system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Use of a qualified medical interpreter
mechanism: Qualified interpretation improves accurate bidirectional communication and protects patient understanding and autonomy when clinician and patient do not share a language.
vignette: A 58-year-old woman who speaks very little English is hospitalized for a newly diagnosed condition. Her 14-year-old daughter speaks English fluently and offers to translate a discussion about treatment options.
lead: Which approach is most appropriate for the physician?
correct: Arrange a qualified interpreter and speak directly to the patient
distractors: Ask the daughter to interpret because she knows the patient best
Proceed in English and ask the daughter to summarize afterward
Limit the discussion to yes-or-no questions so interpretation is unnecessary
Ask the patient to sign consent before obtaining language assistance
distractor_notes: A minor family member should not replace qualified interpretation for complex clinical communication when professional language assistance is available.
The patient needs real-time access to understandable information during the clinical conversation, not only a family summary afterward.
Reducing a complex decision to yes-or-no questions does not resolve the language barrier or ensure informed understanding.
Consent should follow understandable disclosure and communication; obtaining a signature before language access does not establish informed decision-making.
key_expl: When language differences impede communication, the clinician should use qualified interpreter services and continue to address the patient directly.
objective: Choose qualified language assistance rather than relying on family members for complex medical communication.
clues: minor child offering to translate treatment choices

sources.title: Must a covered health care provider obtain an individual’s authorization to use or disclose protected health information to an interpreter?
sources.support: HHS explains that health care providers may use interpreter services to communicate with patients who speak another language and that authorization is not generally required when applicable Privacy Rule conditions are met.

sources.title: Key Strategies for Clear Communication
sources.support: AHRQ explicitly recommends using qualified interpreters as a core clear-communication strategy.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Teach-back evaluates whether the clinician explained information clearly by asking the patient to describe the plan in their own words, allowing misunderstanding to be identified and corrected.
vignette: A physician explains a new insulin regimen to a patient. The patient nods and says, “Yes, I understand.” The physician wants to verify comprehension before the patient leaves.
correct: Ask the patient to explain in their own words how they will use the insulin at home
distractors: Ask, “Do you understand everything I said?” one more time
Give the patient the written instructions and end the visit
Ask the patient to repeat the physician’s sentences word for word
Ask a family member whether the patient usually follows instructions
distractor_notes: A yes-or-no understanding question can miss substantial misunderstanding because patients may answer yes despite confusion.
Written material can reinforce education but does not itself verify comprehension.
Teach-back is not rote repetition; the patient should explain the plan in their own words.
A family member’s opinion about adherence does not demonstrate the patient's current understanding of the new regimen.
key_expl: Teach-back asks the patient to restate the plan in their own words so the clinician can assess the clarity of the explanation and reteach if necessary.
objective: Use teach-back to verify patient understanding without shaming or testing the patient.

sources.title: Tool: Teach-Back
sources.support: AHRQ describes teach-back as asking patients or caregivers to explain needed information or actions in their own words to confirm clear understanding.

sources.title: Use the Teach-Back Method: Tool 5
sources.support: AHRQ recommends non-shaming questions that ask patients to state the plan in their own words and repeating explanation when misunderstanding is found.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Patient-centered adverse-event disclosure promptly communicates known facts, acknowledges harm with empathy, avoids unsupported speculation, explains current care and investigation, and maintains follow-up communication.
vignette: A hospitalized patient receives the wrong dose of a medication and develops transient hypotension. The patient is now stable. The care team has confirmed the medication error but has not yet completed its systems investigation.
lead: Which statement is the most appropriate initial communication with the patient?
correct: Explain that the wrong dose was given, describe what is known about its effects and current care, express sincere regret, and explain that the event will be investigated further
distractors: Wait until the entire investigation is complete before telling the patient anything
State that no error occurred because the patient has recovered
Speculate about which staff member probably caused the error so the patient has an explanation
Provide only the physiologic details of the hypotension and omit that the medication dose was incorrect
distractor_notes: AHRQ's CANDOR approach supports timely initial disclosure rather than withholding the event until every detail is known.
Recovery does not erase the adverse event; honest disclosure is still appropriate.
Initial disclosure should explain known facts without guessing or assigning unsupported blame.
Clear disclosure should identify the adverse event itself, not obscure it behind technical physiologic details.
key_expl: Appropriate initial disclosure is timely, factual, empathetic, explicit about the event, and clear about what is known, current care, and planned investigation.
objective: Communicate transparently and empathetically after a confirmed patient-safety event while avoiding speculation.
clues: patient stable but investigation not complete

sources.title: Disclosure Checklist
sources.locator: Initial Disclosure Conversation; Explain the Facts; Apologize
sources.support: AHRQ recommends advising the patient that an adverse event occurred, explaining known facts and consequences without speculation, expressing sincere regret, and planning follow-up.

sources.title: Communication and Optimal Resolution (CANDOR)
sources.support: AHRQ describes CANDOR as a timely, transparent, patient-centered process for responding when unexpected events cause harm.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: When a capable patient is present, clinicians may share information directly relevant to a family member's involvement in care if the patient agrees, does not object after an opportunity to do so, or circumstances reasonably support that inference.
vignette: A competent adult patient is hospitalized after surgery. His sister is present and helps organize his medications at home. She asks the physician which medication doses have changed. The patient is awake and able to make decisions.
lead: What is the most appropriate next step?
correct: Ask the patient whether he agrees to discussing the relevant medication information with his sister
distractors: Refuse to discuss any health information with family under all circumstances
Give the sister the patient's complete medical record because she helps with medications
Discuss the medication changes without acknowledging the patient because the sister is a relative
Require a notarized written authorization before any relevant discussion can occur
distractor_notes: HIPAA permits relevant communication with people involved in care when the applicable conditions are met; it does not prohibit all family discussions.
Only information directly relevant to the person's involvement should be shared, not the entire medical record by default.
When the capable patient is present, the patient's agreement or opportunity to object should be respected rather than bypassed.
Written notarized authorization is not universally required for these routine care-related disclosures under 45 CFR 164.510(b).
key_expl: Because the capable patient is present, the clinician should involve him and obtain or reasonably establish his agreement before sharing information relevant to his sister's role.
objective: Apply HIPAA rules to communication with family members involved in a capable patient's care.
clues: sister is involved in medication management

sources.title: Does HIPAA allow a health care provider to communicate with a patient’s family, friends, or other persons who are involved in the patient’s care?
sources.support: HHS states that when a capable patient is present, providers may communicate relevant information with involved family or friends if the patient agrees or does not object, with disclosures limited to information relevant to the person's involvement.

sources.title: Does the HIPAA Privacy Rule permit a doctor to discuss a patient’s health status, treatment, or payment arrangements with the patient’s family and friends?
sources.support: HHS explains that relevant information may be shared with family or friends involved in care when the patient agrees, does not object, or nonobjection can reasonably be inferred.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Valid informed consent is an ongoing communication process requiring adequate disclosure, facilitation of understanding, and a voluntary decision rather than merely obtaining a signature.
vignette: An investigator is enrolling adults in a clinical research study. A prospective participant signs the consent form immediately after receiving a dense technical document but cannot explain the study's major risks or alternatives.
lead: Which action is most appropriate before enrollment?
correct: Re-explain the study in understandable language, assess comprehension, and ensure the decision is voluntary before obtaining valid consent
distractors: Enroll the participant because the signed form alone establishes valid consent
Ask a family member to sign instead even though the participant has decision-making capacity
Omit discussion of alternatives because the study has potential benefit
Tell the participant that declining will jeopardize future clinical care
distractor_notes: A signature alone does not replace the informed-consent process of disclosure, understanding, and voluntariness.
A capable adult ordinarily makes their own research decision; substituting a family signature is not justified by poor initial explanation.
HHS informed-consent requirements include disclosure of appropriate alternative procedures or courses of treatment when applicable.
Threatening loss of clinical care undermines voluntariness and is inconsistent with valid consent.
key_expl: The investigator must facilitate understanding and voluntariness after adequate disclosure; inability to explain major information shows the consent process is incomplete despite a signature.
objective: Distinguish genuine informed consent from mere documentation of consent.

sources.title: Informed Consent FAQs
sources.locator: Key features and basic elements of informed consent
sources.support: OHRP identifies disclosure, facilitation of understanding, and voluntariness as core features of the informed-consent process.

sources.title: Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects ('Common Rule')
sources.locator: 45 CFR 46.116 — General requirements for informed consent
sources.support: HHS regulations require legally effective informed consent and specify information and conditions needed for informed, voluntary participation.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: When a child is capable of assent and assent is required by the IRB, assent means affirmative agreement; silence or failure to resist is not sufficient.
vignette: A 12-year-old child is being considered for a minimal-risk research study. The parents give permission. The IRB has determined that children of this age and maturity should provide assent. When the study is explained, the child clearly states, “I do not want to participate.”
correct: Do not enroll the child because required assent has not been obtained
distractors: Enroll the child because parental permission automatically overrides dissent
Enroll the child because remaining in the room counts as assent
Ask the parents to persuade the child until the child stops objecting
Treat the child's silence after the parents speak as affirmative assent
distractor_notes: When capable-child assent is required, parental permission alone does not substitute for the child's affirmative agreement.
HHS regulations define assent as affirmative agreement; passive presence or failure to object is insufficient.
Pressure designed merely to extinguish dissent undermines the purpose of soliciting meaningful assent.
Silence is not affirmative agreement under the federal definition of assent.
key_expl: Because the IRB requires assent and the child is capable of providing it, explicit dissent means the child cannot be enrolled under the stated circumstances.
objective: Apply the federal definition of child assent as affirmative agreement rather than passive nonobjection.

sources.title: Research with Children FAQs
sources.locator: What is child assent?; disagreement between child and parents
sources.support: OHRP defines assent as a child's affirmative agreement and states that mere failure to object is not assent; when required, capable-child assent must be obtained.

sources.title: Subpart D — Additional Protections for Children Involved as Subjects in Research
sources.support: HHS regulations require IRBs to make adequate provisions for soliciting assent from children judged capable of assenting, subject to specified exceptions.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Shared decision making combines evidence about reasonable options with clinician expertise and the informed patient's values and preferences to reach and revisit a treatment decision.
vignette: A patient with a condition has two medically reasonable treatments. One has a higher chance of symptom relief but also a higher risk of a side effect the patient strongly wishes to avoid. The patient asks the physician which option to choose.
lead: Which response best reflects shared decision making?
correct: Compare the benefits and harms of both options, explore what matters most to the patient, and reach a decision together
distractors: Choose the treatment with the highest average efficacy without discussing preferences
List both treatments and tell the patient to decide alone without clinical guidance
Recommend the physician's personal preference because both treatments are medically acceptable
Avoid discussing adverse effects so the patient is not biased against the more effective option
distractor_notes: Shared decision making incorporates patient values rather than selecting solely by population-average efficacy.
Shared decision making is collaborative; it does not abandon the patient to make an unsupported decision.
The clinician's personal preference does not replace the informed patient's goals and values.
Balanced discussion requires meaningful comparison of benefits, harms, and risks rather than withholding material disadvantages.
key_expl: The AHRQ SHARE model calls for inviting participation, comparing options, assessing patient values, reaching a decision together, and evaluating the decision.
objective: Use patient values and evidence about reasonable options to conduct shared decision making.
clues: tradeoff depends on a side effect the patient strongly values avoiding

sources.title: The SHARE Approach Essential Steps of Shared Decision Making
sources.locator: Five steps of shared decision making
sources.support: AHRQ recommends seeking patient participation, comparing options, assessing patient values and preferences, reaching a decision together, and evaluating the decision.

sources.title: The SHARE Approach: Shared Decisionmaking Tools and Training
sources.support: AHRQ describes shared decision making as meaningful dialogue comparing benefits, harms, and risks while considering what matters most to the patient.
